summary: This standards-track RFC defines an IMAP extension where a server tells the client the maximum message size it will accept for upload. Clients can then avoid APPEND commands that would fail because the message is too large.

eli5.summary: The mailbox tells you in advance how big a package it accepts, so you do not carry one that will be refused.

questions: what does the toobig response code mean in imap
how do i find the imap upload size limit
subtitle: An IMAP extension that tells clients the largest message a server will accept before they upload it.

tldr.problem: IMAP servers often limit upload size but do not tell the client, so a client can send a huge message with a non-synchronizing literal and only learn afterwards that the APPEND failed.
tldr.mechanism: The server advertises an APPENDLIMIT capability, either with one value for all mailboxes or without a value, in which case the client reads per-mailbox limits through STATUS or LIST.
tldr.outcome: Clients can skip uploads that would be refused, which saves battery and mobile data. Oversized APPENDs are rejected with a TOOBIG response code.

today: RFC 7889 is a Proposed Standard and the metadata shows it has not been obsoleted or updated, so it remains the definition of the IMAP APPENDLIMIT extension.

sections.title: The Problem and the Idea
sections.content:
Some IMAP servers limit message upload size and do not publish the limit. If a client APPENDs a message with huge attachments using non-synchronizing literals, the APPEND fails because of the limit, but the client has already sent the data. That wastes resources, especially on mobile devices where it consumes battery power and mobile data.

The APPENDLIMIT extension lets the server advertise the maximum upload size so the client knows the limit beforehand, and the server can avoid processing attachments above it.
sections.eli5: Without the sign, you carry a giant box all the way and only then hear 'too big'. The extension puts up the sign.

sections.title: Advertising the Capability
sections.content:
A server that supports the extension includes APPENDLIMIT in its capability list in the authenticated state, and may also advertise it before login. If the capability is omitted, nothing is conveyed about a fixed maximum size. It comes in two forms.

  • APPENDLIMIT=<number> means the same upload limit applies to all mailboxes, for example S: * CAPABILITY IMAP4rev1 ID APPENDLIMIT=257890.
  • APPENDLIMIT with no value means the extension is supported but limits can differ per mailbox, so the client must discover each one with a STATUS or LIST command.

A client implementing the extension should parse both mailbox-specific and global responses, and avoid trying to APPEND mail larger than the advertised limit.
sections.eli5: The sign at the door either says one size for every counter, or says 'ask at each counter'.

sections.title: Per-Mailbox Limits with STATUS and LIST
sections.content:
A server can have mailbox-specific values that are not part of the CAPABILITY response. It can publish a value for each mailbox, or NIL to say that mailbox has no limit. A new STATUS attribute, APPENDLIMIT, retrieves it: C: t1 STATUS INBOX (APPENDLIMIT) is answered by S: * STATUS INBOX (APPENDLIMIT 257890).

If the server advertises LIST-STATUS (RFC 5819), the client can ask for it with LIST "" % RETURN (STATUS (APPENDLIMIT)), and the server MUST recognize the attribute and include a STATUS response for each matching mailbox. If the server does not support the STATUS return option on LIST, the client should use the STATUS command.

Computing the limit should be fast and should not take Access Control Lists (ACLs), quotas or similar information into account. The limit is only part of the policy, so an APPEND smaller than the limit can still fail because of ACLs or quotas.
sections.eli5: You can ask each counter its own size limit. A counter may say 'no limit'. Even a small box can still be turned away for other reasons.

sections.title: Rejecting Oversized Messages
sections.content:
If a client uploads a message larger than the limit for that mailbox, the server SHALL reject the APPEND with a tagged TOOBIG response code. Section 4 of RFC 4469 covers APPEND response codes and their handling.

A client SHOULD avoid non-synchronizing literals (RFC 7888) when the server's maximum upload size is unknown. Section 4.2.2.3 of RFC 4549 describes their use and their risk for disconnected IMAP clients.
sections.eli5: If you bring a too-big box anyway, the clerk says 'TOOBIG'. When you do not know the limit, do not dump the box on the counter before asking.

sections.title: Formal Syntax
sections.content:
The syntax uses ABNF (RFC 5234) and builds on non-terminals from RFC 3501 (capability, status-att) and RFC 4466 (status-att-val). Strings are case insensitive, and implementations MUST accept them that way.

The additions are capability =/ "APPENDLIMIT" ["=" number], status-att =/ "APPENDLIMIT" and status-att-val =/ "APPENDLIMIT" SP (number / nil). The number is the fixed maximum message size in octets. A value of 0 means the server will not accept any APPEND commands for the affected mailboxes.
sections.eli5: The grammar is the rule for how to write the question and answer so both sides read them the same way. Zero means 'nothing is accepted here'.

sections.title: Security and IANA Notes
sections.content:
The extension gives cooperative clients extra information as an optimization and introduces no new security concerns. It does not address abusive clients that try to consume server resources, so servers still have to disconnect or restrict access to clients that behave abusively.

IANA has added APPENDLIMIT to the IMAP Capabilities registry, with this document as the reference.
sections.eli5: The sign only helps people who read it. Someone set on causing trouble still has to be shown the door.
